description:
We are a passionate and ambitious team of Computer and Electrical Engineering enthusiasts, driven by innovation, technology, and real-world problem-solving.

With experience in programming, artificial intelligence, data analysis, and software development, we aim to transform NASA's open data into creative, practical, and impactful solutions.

Our goal is not just to participate in the NASA Space Apps Challenge, but to build an innovative project that stands out on a global level.
summary: FireSync turns two generations of NASA fire satellites into one consistent fire record for the Eastern Mediterranean, 2001–2025. When MODIS records are joined to VIIRS, yearly hotspot counts jump ×4.7 after 2011, yet Aqua MODIS alone shows no break: the jump comes from VIIRS’s 8.2× smaller pixels, not from more fires. Using 400 real NASA FIRMS files (617,502 detections after quality filtering), we showed that no single conversion factor works: VIIRS sees 5.5× more than MODIS by day, 24.9× at night, and 4.8–11.8× depending on the place. FireSync learns a ratio for every 0.25° cell, by month and day/night, and pulls data-poor cells toward the regional ratio (empirical-Bayes shrinkage). On years the model never saw, error fell 32% (2012–2016) and 38% (2022–2025) compared with one constant ratio, and the 2012 break disappeared (Pettitt p = 0.40). Our live web app shows fires on a 3D globe, flies to any region, and gives every number with a reliability rating. This matters because fire managers, researchers and agencies can now compare any month since 2001 on one scale, without mistaking a sensor change for a real trend.
details:
What it does

FireSync merges two generations of NASA fire satellites into one consistent hotspot record for the Eastern Mediterranean (31–43°E, 29–38°N, 10 countries) from 2001 to 2025. The first generation is MODIS on Terra and Aqua (1 km pixels, since 2000). The second is VIIRS on S-NPP (375 m pixels, since 2012). FireSync is both a reproducible method and a live 3D web app.

How it works

Data: 400 NASA FIRMS yearly country files. They contain 929,678 detections inside the study box, and 617,502 remain after quality filters: MODIS confidence ≥ 30, VIIRS nominal or high, vegetation fires only, and persistent industrial heat sources removed.

Grid: we count detections per 0.25° cell, per month, and by day or night. Months with no observation stay unknown and are never set to zero.

Conversion: each cell learns its own VIIRS:MODIS ratio from the 2012–2021 overlap. A cell with few detections is pulled toward the regional ratio (empirical-Bayes shrinkage, r = (V + kR)/(M + k)). The value of k is chosen by leave-one-year-out cross-validation on training years only.

Output: VIIRS-equivalent hotspot counts for every month since 2001, each with a 90% interval and a High/Medium/Low reliability rating.

Evidence

Joining MODIS and VIIRS directly makes the record jump ×4.7 after 2011 (Pettitt p = 0.0012). Aqua alone shows no break over the same years (p = 0.15).

We compared 9 methods on years the model never saw. Against one constant ratio, our cell ratio cut error by 32% on 2012–2016 and by 38% on an independent test, 2022–2025.

No break remains in the harmonized 2001–2025 record (p = 0.40).

Benefits and impact

Civil defence, agriculture and environment agencies, researchers and journalists can compare any month since 2001 on one scale, without mistaking a sensor change for more fire. Every number shows how reliable it is, and areas with too little data show raw counts instead of a guess. The method can be applied to other regions, and to NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 now that S-NPP has ended (2 Nov 2026).

Tools

Data pipeline and statistics: Python (NumPy, pandas, Requests, Matplotlib).

Scientific paper: LaTeX.

3D web app: React, Vite and CesiumJS, with NASA GIBS imagery, hosted on Render.

Reproducibility: every input file has a SHA-256 checksum, and our scripts regenerate every number.

Creativity

Published work uses one conversion factor per country. FireSync learns one for each place, by day and by night, and tells users how far to trust each number. In the app, you search for a region and the globe flies there, shades the region and names it. It then shows a harmonized fire calendar and a layer of the fires that only VIIRS can see.

Factors we considered

Day versus night sensitivity: the ratio is 5.5 by day and 24.9 at night.

34% of VIIRS detections fall where MODIS saw nothing.

Clouds, using NASA POWER data; their link with error is weak (ρ = 0.20).

Industrial heat sources.

Pixel growth away from the satellite track.

Terra and Aqua orbit drift.

Fair comparisons over matched years, and no tuning on test years.

Honest limits: our 90% intervals covered 88% and 81% of cases in testing.

Region boundaries are shown exactly as their sources publish them.
